data.full_text:
ASX-listed Zip Co, which provides digital financial services to consumers in the US, announced on that Column N.A., a nationally chartered bank, will act as a bank partner for its unsecured US instalment lending products. The agreement is Zip’s second banking partnership in the market and extends the bank partnership model through which the company offers credit products to US consumers.
Column N.A. operates under a US national bank charter and is federally regulated. Its addition brings a nationally chartered bank into Zip’s US partner base, which the company presents as part of a wider effort to diversify its banking relationships.
According to Zip, the expanded model is intended to support funding cost efficiencies and strengthen operational resilience. The company ties the move directly to the scale its US business has reached. At the same time, the initiative frames a broader partner structure as a requirement for an operation of its current size rather than an incremental adjustment.
Funding diversification as a growth lever
Rory Herriman, President and Interim CEO at Zip US, said that maintaining a diversified funding platform is central to the company’s ability to serve customers as it continues to grow. The official described the partnership as reinforcing the foundations of the business ahead of its next phase of growth. Furthermore, it is also intended to support the continued expansion of access to what the company describes as transparent and responsible credit for millions of US consumers.
According to Brian Fishbein, Chief Investment Officer at Column N.A., the agreement adds a consumer lender of Zip’s reach to a platform that already supports a range of consumer lending products for financial services firms. The representative indicated that Column expects to support Zip through its technology, particularly as Zip moves into new products and serves new customers.
What the partnership signals
Neither company disclosed financial terms, the lending volume expected to run through the new partnership, or a timeline for any new product launches. Zip also did not name its existing bank partner in the announcement.
The arrangement nonetheless points to two priorities for Zip in the US: reducing dependence on a single banking relationship, and preparing its funding structure for product expansion. Adding a federally regulated, nationally chartered bank also gives the company an additional regulated counterparty for its unsecured lending activity.
For Column N.A., the partnership reflects its focus on providing bank and technology infrastructure to consumer lending businesses operating at scale. The extent to which the new partnership supports Zip’s planned product expansion is likely to become clearer once those products are introduced.

by Editorial Team 43 minutes ago

The card issuing product lets fintechs launch branded debit and credit card programs without needing a separate card processor. Global banking accounts extend Column’s reach beyond US borders, while multicurrency accounts allow clients to hold and transact in multiple currencies from a single integration point. data.title: Column Just Ate the Card Processor: A Self-Funded Bank Shows Where Stablecoin Spend Margin Concentrates
data.ai_summary: Column, a self-funded national bank, launched stablecoin transactions and full-stack card issuing, consolidating bank, processor, and capital roles. It reported $153 million in 2025 revenue, up 219% year over year, with $83 million from interest income and $70 million from interchange. The move signals where stablecoin card margins concentrate, with networks like Visa and Mastercard as the investable exposure.
data.author: Adrian Savafollow
data.full_text: The card in your wallet is never really one thing. Pull it apart and you find a bank that holds the account and the network license, a processor that authorizes and settles transactions, and often a separate lender that fronts the credit or capital. For the fintech companies that build those cards, the default was to stitch all three together from independent vendors and hand each one a slice of the economics — a sponsor bank here, a processor there, a capital provider somewhere else. Last week a company you've never heard of announced it was sinking the seams. Column — a nationally chartered bank that acts as software infrastructure for other fintechs and says it moved more than $4.5 trillion last year — launched stablecoin transactions, full-stack card issuing, global banking, and multicurrency accounts in a single release. Its founder, Plaid co-founder William Hockey, called it "completing the stack". The point is that a fintech card program no longer needs a bank, a processor, and a capital partner at all; Column says it is now all three, in one FDIC-member entity that owns its own card numbers. The structural move matters beyond one private company, because Column is the infrastructure-company equivalent of a tell: it shows where the margin in the fastest-growing payment category is concentrating, and who is positioned to capture it. Why owning the charter changes the arithmetic Start with what Column actually is, because the difference from its competitors is the whole story. Column N.A. is not a processor renting a bank's license. It is a national bank, member FDIC, founded in 2021 when the founders put roughly $50 million of their own money into buying Northern California National Bank and rebuilt it as an API-first platform. A directory of the nineteen major card-issuing platforms in the U.S. sorts the field by three things: license structure, network access, and who actually holds the bank identification number, the BIN. On all three, Column sits in the top category — the group of "global infrastructure" providers that hold their own licenses and BINs, alongside Cross River, Green DotGDOT--, and Pathward — rather than the processors (Lithic, Marqeta, Galileo) or orchestrators (Unit, Synctera) that depend on someone else's sponsorship and split the fees accordingly. That ownership is the economic engine. In the old banking-as-a-service model, a card program's revenue is carved up between the middleware platform, the sponsor bank, and the capital provider. Column breaks that fragmentation by being all of them: it takes deposits, so it earns the interest; it issues and processes cards, so it keeps the interchange and usage fees; and it offers its own lending balance sheet, so the credit economics stay inside too. Sacra estimates Column's revenue reached about $153 million in 2025, up 219% year over year, with roughly $83 million from interest income on deposits and $70 million from interchange and usage-based charges. The math is the strategy: the less you have to share, the more of every dollar of client activity is yours. The stablecoin card is the part to watch Column's card launch on its own would be a consolidation story. Its stablecoin piece is what turns it into a growth story, because that is where the volume is exploding. Stablecoin-linked cards are the bridge that turns crypto holdings into ordinary merchant spending. Instead of the merchant accepting crypto, the card converts a USDC or USDT balance into dollars at the point of sale on the Visa and Mastercard rails, settling outside banking hours. Retail spending through these cards has roughly doubled in the past year; card-based stablecoin volume grew about 106% year over year, reaching an annualized rate of roughly $18 billion by early 2026. It is still a rounding error against global card spend — under 1% — but it is growing like a breakout category, and a national bank that holds the whole stack, settled in USDC against the dollar across U.S. and international rails, is positioned to keep that margin rather than hand it to a processor. There is a genuine moat in regulatory form here. A pure stablecoin processor can build the rails, but it cannot custody the dollars or hold the deposit base the way a chartered bank can. Column's pitch is that its clients get stablecoin interoperability and card acceptance without abandoning the safety and regulatory envelope of an insured bank. For a retail investor, the honest reading is that the stablecoin card rail is real and compounding, and the companies that will capture it are the ones that own a charter, the network access, and a balance sheet at once — not the middleware that rents them. What should give a retail investor pause The case for the category is not a case for Column as a position, because you cannot buy it. The company is entirely founder- and employee-owned, with no venture investors and no public shares. So the useful questions are what it signals and which investable exposures capture the same tailwind. The first caution is concentration. Column's revenue is tied to a small set of marquee clients — Mercury, Brex, Ramp, Bilt, Slash, plus lending partners like Propel and Best Egg. That has been the growth engine, but it means the whole business leans on a handful of fintechs that could churn, consolidate, or blow up. The second is that nearly half its 2025 revenue was interest income on deposits, a number that rises and falls with the rate cycle rather than with product adoption. For a shareholder-oriented takeaway, the cleanest public counterparty to the stablecoin card boom is not Column — it is the networks themselves. Every one of these cards, Column's included, runs on Visa or Mastercard and pays them a fee on each transaction, and the still-tiny share of card spend these stablecoin products represent is the headroom. A self-funded bank deciding it needs to own the processor it used to route through is a signal about where payments margin is going; the investor who wants that exposure without taking on a private bank's math may find the network that collects tolls on every card to be the sturdier bet. Column's launch is a reminder that the payment stack you thought was fixed is being rebuilt from the inside, and that in the stablecoin era the people who win own the whole thing — the charter, the rails, and the balance sheet. The rest are hoping to be paid to stand in the middle.

News Column Stablecoin Platform Connects USDC, USDT with Global Payment Rails Column has launched four financial infrastructure products covering stablecoins, card issuing, global banking, and multicurrency accounts. The platform supports 24/7 USDC and USDT conversion and connects digital dollars with bank accounts and domestic and international payment rails.

Written By: Kelvin Munene Reviewed By: Manisha Sharma









Copied Column has launched four infrastructure products that connect stablecoins, card issuing, global banking and multicurrency accounts through one banking platform. The rollout, announced on September 16, allows fintech companies to use USDC and USDT alongside bank accounts, cards and payment networks . Column co-founder William Hockey said the launch completes a multi-year effort to build the company’s technology stack. In a company post, Hockey said, “We have finally completed that build.” He added that the products are already handling billions of dollars for fintech companies, including Ramp, Brex, Bilt, Mercury, Slash and Kapital. Column Connects USDC and USDT with Bank Payment Rails Column’s stablecoin service lets businesses send and receive USDC and USDT while converting funds to and from US dollars at any time. The company said it built the service directly into its banking core, so customers do not need to prefund balances with a separate provider before making a stablecoin transfer. The platform connects stablecoin activity with US and international payment rails. The company gave an example of a business receiving USDC from Mongolia and converting the funds into dollars. The business could then split the money, send one portion to a US community bank through FedNow and convert another into euros for a SWIFT payment. Column said the process can take place within seconds through its APIs. The service operates 24 hours a day, including weekends and holidays. Card Issuing Combines Banking, Processing and Capital Column also launched a card issuing product after building its own issuer processor. The service brings the issuing bank, processing system, and capital into one integration. Column said customers can use the platform to create credit, debit, prepaid, and stablecoin-backed card programs on the Visa and Mastercard networks . The company had sponsored card programs before adding its processing system. By controlling the processing layer, Column can manage card authorization and settlement within the same system that supports its banking products. This reduces the number of separate providers fintech companies need when launching card programs. Column said its processor has direct connections to Visa and Mastercard and runs on the same core infrastructure used for its other banking services. Global Banking and Multicurrency Accounts Expand Payment Options The third product extends Column’s account and card infrastructure to verified customers outside the United States. Businesses can offer US dollar or local currency accounts and cards to eligible users in other markets while using the same compliance tools and APIs used for domestic customers. However, Column did not publish a full list of supported countries, so availability depends on its banking and verification coverage. Column also introduced multicurrency accounts that allow customers to receive, hold, and send foreign currencies. The company said users can convert supported currencies to and from US dollars instantly and connect payments to international systems, including SEPA Instant. Supported currencies include euros, British pounds and Canadian dollars, among others. Together, the four products allow fintech companies to connect stablecoins, bank accounts, cards and foreign currency payments through one platform. Column said the services can work together because they use the same underlying infrastructure. The company did not provide separate transaction volumes for each product, but Hockey said the services are already moving billions of dollars for fintech customers. data.ai_summary: Rent fintech Flex has applied with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and Utah Department of Financial Institutions for an industrial loan company charter to become an industrial bank, the company announced Friday. data.author: Dan Ennis
data.full_text: Rent fintech Flex has applied with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and Utah Department of Financial Institutions to become an industrial bank, the company announced Friday. “A bank charter allows us to build directly on a foundation of federal deposit insurance and full state and federal bank regulatory oversight, strengthening the products millions of renters already rely on,” Shragie Lichtenstein, CEO and co-founder of Flex, said in a statement. “Rent is the single biggest bill in most people’s lives, and it’s often the one least adapted to how they’re actually paid. This charter gives us a permanent, regulated foundation to keep closing that gap.” Jeff Berkson – who until May served as chief risk officer at WebBank, according to LinkedIn – will be Flex Bank’s proposed CEO. The bank will be based in the Salt Lake City area and operate nationally through digital channels. The bank would issue Flex’s core credit products, including the flexible payment solution Flex Rent, directly to customers. Flex has processed more than $40 billion in rent since 2019 for more than 3.2 million users, and has helped them avoid more than $780 million in late fees, the company said, adding that it does not compound interest or permit the stacking of loans. Trump-era regulators have seen a sharp increase in new charter applications. FDIC Chair Travis Hill last year touted the industrial loan company charter as one of a handful of ways to boost the establishment of new banks. Buy now, pay later juggernaut Klarna applied this month for an ILC charter. Car maker Stellantis received approval in May to launch an ILC and other automotive stalwarts, including Ford and GM, got green lights in January. Investment firm Edward Jones followed in February. Some lawmakers, with backing from the banking industry, have argued that an ILC charter exempts companies from the definition of a “bank” under the Bank Holding Company Act. As long as ILCs don’t offer demand deposit accounts, they can bypass oversight by the Federal Reserve, the politicians contend. In January, Sens. John Kennedy, R-LA, and Andy Kim, D-NJ, introduced a bill to close what they called the “shadow banking loophole.” The bill is now sitting with the Senate Banking Committee. Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Banking Dive free daily newsletter The trade group Independent Community Bankers of America said in May that cutting the Fed out of ILC supervision “leav[es] a dangerous gap in safety and soundness oversight and introducing unnecessary systemic risk into the banking system.” Last year, Kim and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-MA, proposed a moratorium on commercially owned ILC charters until such entities are defined as “banks” under the BHC Act. The ILC isn’t the only charter that has seen refreshed interest since President Donald Trump reentered the White House. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has seen an uptick in applications for national trust charters, popular among cryptocurrency firms. A handful of fintechs – including Upstart, Mercury and Valt Bank – have opted to try for full bank charters. Flex currently uses Lead Bank and Column Bank as its sponsor banks. An ILC charter for Flex would make those partnerships unnecessary.
